## What is a postdoc?

A researcher with a doctorate, working on a fixed-term contract or stipend, not yet counted as independent staff [@eurodoc2025].

There is no consensual definition across institutions or countries. The label covers people two months and twenty years past their PhD.

## Why this stage exists

Postdoctoral positions are meant to bridge doctoral training and an independent research career: time to publish, build a network, and win the grants a permanent post requires.

Nature describes postdocs as "the overlooked segment of the scientific workforce" [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

## Who becomes a postdoc

Of the 3,838 respondents to Nature's 2023 global survey: 51% women, 47% men; 27% an ethnic or racial minority in their country of work; 61% working outside their home country [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

Regionally, the sample skews toward Europe (45%) and North and Central America (38%), with Asia, Africa, Australasia, and South America together making up the rest [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

## Job satisfaction, overall

55% of postdocs describe themselves as satisfied with their current position, down slightly from 60% in 2020 [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

Satisfaction varies by geography: 68% satisfied in Australasia and 58% in Europe, against 38% dissatisfied in Africa and 34% in North and Central America [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

## What satisfies and what doesn't

| Most satisfied with | % satisfied | Least satisfied with | % satisfied |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interest in the work | 75% | Job security | 29% |
| Degree of independence | 73% | Career-advancement opportunities | 34% |
| Interesting projects | 72% | Availability of funding | 37% |
| Feeling safe in the workplace | 72% | Management and leadership | 39% |

The pattern has held since 2020: postdocs like the work itself and dislike its stability [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

## The contract treadmill

41.5% of European postdocs have already held three or more temporary research contracts. 78.7% have less than two years left on their current one. Only 1.2% hold a permanent contract [@eurodoc2025].

## Access to social security

Only 20% of European postdocs have full access to healthcare, parental leave, pension, sick leave, and unemployment benefits combined. 13.1% have none of the five [@eurodoc2025].

The gap runs north to south: 32.5% of postdocs in Western Europe have full coverage, against 9.5% in Southern Europe [@eurodoc2025].

## Salary and the second job

Most postdocs report earning $50,000–$79,999 a year, but the range is wide: 88% in Australasia and 86% in North and Central America earn over $50,000, while 78% in Africa and 78% in South America earn under $30,000 [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

10% now hold a second job, up from 6% in 2020, mostly for extra income (72%) and concentrated in Africa (33%) and South America (28%) [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023]. Only 20% can save what they want to, down from 29% in 2020 [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

## Mobility as the default

74% of European postdocs have lived in two or more countries since their master's degree; 54% of Nature's respondents moved to a new country specifically for their current postdoc [@eurodoc2025; @researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

Mobility is uneven: postdocs in Northern and Western Europe move the most, while 56% of those in Southern Europe stay at the institution where they did their PhD [@eurodoc2025].

## The two-body problem

16% of European postdocs live apart from their partner or commute between countries for work [@eurodoc2025].

> "We have one big move left. We won't move any more for postdocs." — Manuel Chevalier, after eight years of postdocs in three countries [@nordling2023thirties]

## Postdocs in their thirties

Postdocs aged 31–40 are more negative than those under 30 about job prospects, job security, and work–life balance, and more likely to report mental-health challenges [@nordling2023thirties].

Dissatisfaction also compounds with time in the role: 34% of those on their third or fourth postdoc report dissatisfaction, against 24% of those on their first [@nordling2023thirties].

## Mentorship and career support

Only 23% of European postdocs feel their institution gives them enough guidance on career options, and 37% report no career support office at all [@eurodoc2025].

Supervisor contact time is often thin: 49% of postdocs get less than an hour a week, though this has improved slightly since 2020 (55%) [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

## Discrimination and harassment

24% of postdocs report experiencing discrimination or harassment in a current or previous position — unchanged from 2020. Bullying is the most common form [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

Those who are female, an ethnic minority in their country of work, or living with a disability are consistently more likely to report it [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

## Mental health and work-life balance

52% of postdocs have considered leaving science because of anxiety, depression, or related concerns [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023]. In Europe, 53% report an imbalance between work and non-work life [@eurodoc2025].

The reasons cluster around precarity itself: uncertain job opportunities (58.5%), temporary contracts (58.6%), and lack of stable income (41.9%) [@eurodoc2025].

## The puzzle {.statement}

65% of postdocs plan to base their career in academia. It is "extremely unlikely that 65% will end up in tenured or in long-term academic positions in their fields" [@nordling2023optimism].

## Industry versus academia

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Academia**

- 54% satisfied
- 5% earn $80,000–$110,000
- 12% avoid all overtime
- 74% feel physically safe at work
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Industry**

- 65% satisfied
- 23% earn $80,000–$110,000
- 20% avoid all overtime
- 83% feel physically safe at work
:::

::::

Source: [@nordling2023optimism]

## Career optimism after COVID

Optimism about future careers rose from 28% of respondents in 2020 to 41% in 2023, and COVID-19 fell from the top concern (40%) to a minor one (8%) [@nordling2023optimism].

What replaced it: competition for funding, scarce jobs in one's field, and pressure to sacrifice personal time for work [@nordling2023optimism].

## The recruitment paradox {.question}

If postdocs are this dissatisfied, why are institutions struggling to fill the positions?

44% of postdocs are aware of struggles to fill postdoc vacancies in their own workplace, most often citing a lack of career stability as the reason [@researchNaturePostDoctoralSurvey2023].

## Postdocs organizing

Postdocs in the United States and elsewhere have gone on strike at several universities, and discussions of a national postdoc union are ongoing [@nordling2023optimism].

> "There's a lot of work to be done. And none of us can do it alone." — Tim MacKenzie, genetics postdoc, Stanford [@nordling2023optimism]

## What stable employment could look like

Standard employment contracts of a reasonable minimum length, such as two years or longer, rather than serial short-term renewal [@eurodoc2025].

Eurodoc proposes mandatory Sustainable Career Plans for research institutions, modeled on the European Commission's Gender Equality Plans [@eurodoc2025].

## What a fair career pathway looks like

Clear roles, rights, and responsibilities from the start of the contract, and recognition of postdocs as a distinct staff category rather than a residual one [@eurodoc2025].

A common, transparent research career framework across Europe, recognizing the postdoc years as professional experience and opening flexible pathways in and out of academia [@eurodoc2025].

## Open questions {.question}

If the field can only place one in five postdocs permanently, what should the other four be told, and by whom?
